name: 艾努语 Äynu / Eynu
confidence_why: The only statement on Äynu stress is a Chinese Wikipedia summary of Zhao Xiangru and Aximu's 2011 grammar (pp. 34-36), which itself calls the position in disyllables unfixed and gives only tendencies for longer and suffixed words, while Çakmak 2015, Liang 2020, Tursun 2007 and Johanson 2001 say nothing about stress at all, so the record rests on a single second-hand report that no other work confirms.

catalog_quote: 艾努语的读音有六种类型，在一个音节中，元音前最多有一个辅音，元音后最多可以有两个辅音。双音节的词重音位置不确定，多音节有时落到倒数第二个音节上，词汇接词缀时重音会向后移动，通常落在最后一个音节上

new_statements.translation: Äynu has six syllable types; within a syllable there is at most one consonant before the vowel and at most two after it. In disyllabic words the position of the stress is not fixed; in polysyllabic words it sometimes falls on the penultimate syllable; when a word takes suffixes the stress moves rightward, usually falling on the final syllable.

The Harvnb target 赵相如等 2011 resolves in the article's 图书 list (line 134) to 赵相如 & 阿西木, 艾努语研究, 北京: 民族出版社, 2011.03, ISBN 978-7-105-11364-4, i.e. Glottolog's ranked grammar (id 657495); the ref-name prefix "简志" is only the compilers label, the b…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Second-hand summary of Zhao & Aximu 2011: stress position in bare disyllables is variable (not fixed), polysyllables sometimes carry penultimate stress, and suffixed words shift stress rightward so that it usually lands on the last syllable (the Uyghur-type pattern). No single fixed rule is stated; the primary source has not been seen.
new_statements.exceptions: Disyllabic words with 'undetermined' stress position; polysyllables only 'sometimes' penultimate.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (bare words vs. suffixed words); nothing said about phrase-level accent or citation forms. Reported by a tertiary source (Wikipedia) citing a primary grammar in Chinese; treat as provisional until Zhao & Aximu 2011: 34-36 is read.
new_statements.identity_note: The second-hand statement (via Zhao & Aximu 2011) covers Äynu/Eynu in general (ainu1251), described as an Uyghur-based mixed/secret language; Hayasi's material is specifically the Šäyxil (Xinjiang, near Kashgar) variety, which would fall under Glottolog's West Ejnu dialect [west3009]; Memtimin 2020 covers Šayχil, Tameɣil and Givoz.

sources.note: Sect. 4.1 Ses Bilgisi (pp. 1485-1486): 8 vowels, 22 consonants (identical to Uyghur), narrowing of a/e to i, final r-drop, six syllable types CV CVC CVCC V VC VCC (after Hayasi et al. 1999: 23-25; Lee-Smith 1996: 852). No 'vurgu' (stress) statement anywhere in the article.
